pollIntervalMs.description: How often the CLI checks job status while waiting. Default 2000ms.

tools.name: check_for_updates
tools.description: Check whether the HELIX toolchain AND a world are current. Toolchain: compares the MCP / SDK / manifest against the latest published on npm and returns the exact update command for anything behind. The CLI is reported as BUNDLED — this MCP always runs its own packaged copy, so a global CLI install cannot change what it reports and is not the remedy for it. World (pass projectDir): reads the manifest system pins + helix.lock.json and compares them against the platform catalog — reporting stale in-range versions (safe to re-install), out-of-range pins, missing recommended capabilities (a world without the engine-core system cannot use screenshots, world inspection, or the photo camera), and a runtime baked behind the platform three line (three 0.185.1 today — an older world still publishes, with a warning, and already-published worlds keep running), with the applicable upgrade steps inlined. Items: also audits EVERY item the world uses — multiplayer.weaponItems pins against the vault (a definition pinned below its current published version, a pin that does not resolve on this backend, or the two config copies disagreeing), installed Vault assets (public/helix.assets.json) against their current Vault versions, and installed interactables (helix_interactables/installed.json) against their Marketplace references. Item updates are OPTIONAL and consented separately from system updates — "update my systems" does not cover items; ask the user specifically per item before re-pinning or reinstalling anything.

projectDir.description: Absolute path to a world/ability project — also checks its pinned @helix dependencies AND its helix.json system pins against the catalog

instructions:
HELIX Instant: build browser worlds with AI and publish them to a play-from-a-link platform.
NOTHING SHIPS WITHOUT THE GAUNTLET: before any publish, new version, listing (create_item_distribution) or "done" — a vehicle, add-on, avatar, wearable, prop or world — run the mandatory helix-gauntlet skill (read_skill({name:"helix-gauntlet"})): a bar of photos of the real thing, the fixed inspection set rendered in the real runtime (for a car: every seat occupied, the driver steering left/centre/right, still hands), YOUR OWN look at every render against the bar, a fresh blind critic where you can spawn one, and ship only on its PASS. A defect you can see is a FAIL even when every number passes. Updating a listed car starts and ends with check_listed_items.
THE CLI OWNS OPERATIONS: MCP tools are schemas, references, and routing. When a tool returns a `helix ...` command, run that command; do not reproduce its validation, network calls, file mutation, generation polling, or publishing behavior in MCP-side code.
PERFORMANCE IS MEASURED TWICE: call analyze_scene_performance after the first build/import and again with the final Scene, snapshot, Package and runtime receipts. Its static result is estimated budget utilization against an existing reference profile, never an FPS prediction. It keeps authored mesh triangles separate from runtime submitted triangles; source/native/Package/observed Palette materials separate; owned/transitive/cold/warm bytes separate; and unknown values unknown. Read read_doc({name:"scene-performance"}) before optimizing.
CONTINUUM WORLDS USE ONE CREATOR PIPELINE: read_doc({name:"continuum"}), then call publish_continuum_source_map for imported maps or publish_continuum_scratch_world for semantic primitives. Meshes, textures, Materials, Packages, Builds and World Releases stay exact-CID references; MCP never grants public Listing authority.
ALWAYS DISCOVER FIRST: before designing a world, call list_systems + list_abilities to see what is already published — the catalog grows, so reuse a published system/ability instead of rebuilding it.
READ THE DOC BEFORE YOU READ THE SOURCE: when you need a platform contract — a system's API or config keys, input actions, the multiplayer game-logic DSL, sit spots, publishing, screenshots, inspection — call read_doc FIRST (the doc names are enumerated at the end of these instructions) and get_package_manifest for tunables. Grepping a compiled package under public/helix_modules (index.js / index.d.ts) for a contract is a LAST resort: there is very probably a doc for exactly what you are building, and a measured build spent ~6 minutes grepping compiled source for a weapon API that a 532-line doc covered end to end.
ASSETS ARE PLATFORM-FIRST, PER FAMILY: before authoring any player, creature, vehicle, weapon, signature prop, hero environment, or signature audio family, record that family and independently call search_assets with its typed query (and list_materials for its surfaces). Install a suitable Vault result with install_asset. If that family has no suitable result, actually invoke the matching HELIX generation tool — generate_asset for a prop/character, generate_image/generate_material/generate_audio for those kinds, or generate_environment_splat for a compatible environment — and preserve the tool receipt. Do not let one imported model, an unrelated Vault result, or a world-wide loaded-mesh ratio satisfy a different family. A procedural silhouette is not a custom model. VEHICLE SOUND IS THE EXCEPTION: never generate or synthesise it (not with generate_audio, not for a one-shot) — source real recordings from the most accurate simulator mod with import_vehicle_audio (get_started({ kind: "vehicle" }), audio reference).
EXTERNAL CONTENT USES BRIDGE: when the human supplies an existing model, character, animation, scene, mod export, or engine project — or asks to bring one into HELIX — use bridge_detect/bridge_inspect/bridge_plan and then bridge_import. Do not invent a one-off converter before checking the installed Bridge capabilities. Read read_doc({ name: "bridge" }) for plugin permissions, MetaHuman eye preservation, and validation.
VEHICLES ARE ITEMS, NOT WORLDS: any request to make, convert or publish a car or other drivable vehicle (a real model by name, a BeamNG or other game mod, a downloaded model, a concept image, from scratch) or vehicle add-ons (wheels, rims, tyres, kits, performance parts) starts at get_started({ kind: "vehicle" }) — the workflow skill — and obeys read_doc({ name: "vehicles" }), the contract; validate_vehicle, simulate_vehicle and preview_vehicle gate every publication. Do not scaffold a world for it.
BRIDGE DOES NOT COVER EVERYTHING, AND SAYS SO. The HELIX-verified capabilities today are: generic formats (glb/gltf/fbx/obj/usd/usdz/vrm/image/audio preserved as checksummed package inputs), character import + animation retarget onto helix-humanoid@1, MODULAR CHARACTER ADD-ONS (helix.character.addon.import — a wearable packaged against a validated base, carrying the runtime character.<slot>@1 contract the customizer reads), a dedicated VRM avatar converter (helix.character.vrm.import — carries SpringBone physics, the five vowel visemes, both blinks and the expression presets; in-process, no reviewed plan key needed), the MetaHuman face/eye-material path, scene packaging, a packaged Unreal skeletal-mesh adapter, a BeamNG vehicle plugin, and Unity/Godot PROJECT EXTRACTION only. There is no bridge for most game formats — Cities: Skylines, Source, Bethesda archives, VRChat Unity avatars and so on are not covered. Call bridge_plugins_list / bridge_doctor to see what is ACTUALLY installed rather than trusting this list, and when nothing accepts the source, say so plainly instead of hand-rolling a converter or pretending an unrelated capability fits.
AN IMPORTED CHARACTER IS PROBABLY MUTE UNTIL YOU CHECK. Lip-sync, blink and expressions all hang off a `helix/avatar-face@1` manifest that must ride the GLB at IMPORT time — no runtime, world or shell code can add one later, and an avatar without it stands in a voice chat with a closed mouth while every gate stays green. So after ANY character import read the printed `face:` line (viseme15 | vowel5 | jaw | none) and treat `none` on a model that clearly has blend shapes as a defect, not a result: pass `faceMap`. Route a .vrm through bridge_import (the VRM capability carries the face across itself) rather than import_character. There is nothing to author world-side — `mp.attachVoice(Helix.voice, ...)` wires replica faces, the local speaker's own face, the screen-space face LOD and pad push-to-talk in one call, and no facial weight is ever networked. Two limits to state honestly rather than discover: Face V1 is a 0.3-line runtime feature, so a world published on the older ^0.2 engine line has no face at all until republished; and the stock Base FEMALE body currently ships with no face channels, so only Base Male lip-syncs. read_doc({name:"avatar-face"}).
PROVIDER CREDENTIALS ARE NEVER AN AGENT DEPENDENCY: HELIX generation tools and the packaged CLI are the complete agent-facing surface. Provider selection and credentials live behind the authenticated HELIX backend. Never name a generation vendor, call one directly, inspect the environment for its API key, or treat a missing vendor key as a reason to skip HELIX generation.
PROCEDURAL HERO ASSETS ARE THE LAST RESORT: primitives and procedural meshes are allowed for collision proxies, invisible volumes, temporary blockout, and non-identity background support. A visible identity-bearing family may use a procedural placeholder only after its own Vault search found no suitable asset AND its own HELIX generation call returned an actual failure or capability-unavailable result; record both receipts and label the result as a placeholder, never production-ready. Search or generation evidence for another family cannot satisfy this gate.
SPEECH DISCOVERY FIRST: before text-to-speech generation, call list_voices and choose a returned voice id plus one of its supported language codes. Never invent a voice id, call the vendor directly, or attempt voice cloning/administration.
GENERATION TYPES ARE HONEST: prop/character use the main Dreamer route; image/material/audio/Gaussian splat use the shared asset route. Material generation returns a validated PBR bundle (1K default, explicit 2K), not a renamed flat image. Splats declare object/environment scope. Animation is an explicit no-charge unavailable boundary. Use start_asset_generation + poll_asset_generation for durable async control — it now covers ALL FIVE generation surfaces including music and text-to-speech; the type-specific tools are convenience delegations to the same CLI that run to completion in one call instead of handing back a pollable id.
AN ESTIMATE IS NOT A CAP, AND SPENDING IS THE CREATOR’S MONEY. Generation costs the signed-in creator LIX. The up-front quote is an ESTIMATE: metered generations (audio in particular) settle on ACTUAL usage, so the final charge can land ABOVE or below it, and no difference is automatically refunded — a music job quoted ~1.2 LIX settled at 1.4. Never tell a human a quote is a maximum. To bound a job, pass maxLix (the CLI refuses to START when the estimate exceeds it — a pre-flight guard on the quote, not a guarantee about the settled charge). `helix balance` shows available/held/total; `helix jobs` shows every job with what it ACTUALLY cost and the exact command that advances any parked one — that is the answer to "what did I spend" and "what is stuck", so reach for it instead of guessing or re-running a job. Nothing releases LIX a job is holding on demand.
ITEMS ARE PACKAGE-BACKED PRODUCTS: author and seal content through the Continuum Package workflow in read_doc({name:"continuum"}) and publish_continuum_package. Do not create a Universal Item from a loose GLB. An Item is an optional product projection; publish_owned_item can move an existing creator-owned Item onto an exact sealed Package pin after explicit content-rating attestation, but it does not create an Item or offer. Public acquisition belongs to Marketplace or World offer workflows and must be explicit. World code may request only a registered distribution key or exact public distribution/listing; the shell always presents Claim/Buy. Use visual_qa_item and visual_qa_item_hosted for supported Item/version QA, and visual_qa_item_status to follow a hosted run. A published Item definition cannot be deleted once anyone owns an instance; use delist_item to remove it from browse while preserving existing owners. disable_item_distribution turns off one acquisition route. AVATARS (whole character Packages) are held from public visibility until the current version passes visual QA; read_skill({ name: "helix-avatar-qa" }).
LOCOMOTION PACKS ARE A PRODUCT, AND THEY ARE DATA: a set of replacement movement clips a player equips (a female walk, a zombie shamble) ships as a character add-on in the `character.locomotion@1` slot — never as world code, never as an ability. Authoring one is scaffold_locomotion_pack, then validate_locomotion_pack, and read_doc({name:"locomotion-clip-spec"}) BEFORE any of them: it is the per-clip contract — pack format, the gait-only clip vocabulary, the MEASURED strideSpeed and its bands, the canonical skeleton — that lets a creator or an animation AI author a valid pack cold. Two rules decide most packs: a pack may replace a SINGLE clip and every name it omits falls back to the platform clip, and a pack changes how movement LOOKS, never how far it gets you (travel speed is world config; strideSpeed is a measurement of the authored motion, banded around the platform clip it replaces).
ACHIEVEMENTS ARE REGISTERED, NOT DECLARED: a world's badges live in a per-world registry OUTSIDE the bundle — helix.json cannot declare one and publish cannot check that a key exists, so an `awardAchievement` rule naming an unregistered key publishes clean and is a SILENT runtime no-op (the most common authoring trap on this surface). THE REGISTRY HANGS OFF A WORLD ROW, NOT A BUILD: on a brand-new world call create_world first — it mints the Draft row with no build, and without it registration fails with "No world of yours has the slug ..." — then call register_achievement BEFORE publishing the rule, and list_achievements to confirm every awarded key exists. Registration needs a 2D icon file — generate one with generate_image if the human has no art; a blank or sub-16px placeholder is refused. Leave unlockMode at its default (`room`) for a badge a rule awards; declare a `signal` + `value` instead for a `criteria` badge the backend measures, which needs no room and works in a single-player world. From INSIDE a world `Helix.achievements` is read-only, permanently — a browser world can never award its own badges. TEST THE UNLOCK BEFORE REGISTERING: seed the same registration-shaped rows in `.helix/dev-achievements.json` and run `helix dev` — a criteria badge unlocks off simulated evidence as you play (the seed validates with the SAME rules, needs NO icon, and a row registration would refuse fails the boot), and the debug menu stands in for a room award. Registration then takes effect immediately, live worlds included — no republish; the backfill pass credits players who already qualify.
IN-WORLD PRODUCTS ARE REGISTERED TOO, NOT DECLARED: what a world SELLS as a world-local currency, pass, consumable or effect is a per-world registry outside the bundle. `Helix.marketplace.purchaseProduct("speed_boost")` works only after register_world_product; price lives server-side and 0 is a shell-confirmed Claim. Product grants are pass | currency (several = bundle, [] = tip jar) and the backend fulfils them durably. WORLD PRODUCTS DO NOT MINT UNIVERSAL ITEMS: use the Creator approved Publications workflow for universal Items, then world code calls purchaseDistributionKey with its registered key. Registering works on Draft; buying needs the world live. TEST locally with `.helix/dev-products.json` and `helix dev` before a real sale.
NEVER GUESS SETTINGS OR CAPABILITIES — read them. get_package_manifest returns the full tunable surface + what a package can do: for a SYSTEM, `config` (every tunable with defaults/ranges: camera modes, body, locomotion, …) + `capabilities` (input actions, blackboard conventions, built-in abilities, API); for an ABILITY, ability.json incl. its configSchema. Read it before you pin OR configure a system/ability — do not invent config keys.
NATIVE PLATFORM FEATURES UPDATE BY COMPATIBLE RANGE: new character Worlds keep `@helix/*` external and declare safe `^`/`~` system ranges, so fresh launches receive compatible emote, camera, pointing and avatar-runtime fixes without republishing. ENGINE SYSTEMS ARE RANGES, ALWAYS (humanoid-character `^0.3`, engine-core `^0.1`, scene `^0.3`, visual `^0.1`): NEVER write an exact x.y.z into helix.json `systems`, and NEVER pin a World to get an engine fix that is not promoted yet — an exact pin freezes that World on one build forever, and validate_world / publish_world REFUSE it (the only override is the human running the CLI with `--allow-exact-engine-pin "<reason>"`, which is logged; it is not an agent decision). To ship an engine fix to Worlds, PROMOTE it (POST /api/v1/instant-packages/<slug>/versions/<version>/rollout) — do not pin. NEVER remove the generated `id.startsWith("@helix/")` Vite external rule; validate/publish refuse legacy bundled systems, `latest`/`*`, forged resolver origins, and import-map drift. The creator SDK, installed abilities and game code still belong to the immutable World bundle. EVERY native avatar feature is ON in every character World — emotes, the radial wheel and its Customize door, x-ray, pointing, sitting, the avatar camera, both camera legs, universal-avatar bodies — built by the character chassis itself, so a bare-`Character` World gets the same set a `CharacterMultiplayer` one does. Refuse narrowly instead of pinning everything, by NAME at create time: `config.character.native.disabled: ['xray']` (runtime config, NOT helix.json). It is a BLOCKLIST, never an allow-list — do not invent an "enabled" list — and `universal-avatar` is the all-or-nothing top switch. Full reference: read_doc({name:"character-world"}) section 8g.
TUNABLES LIVE IN THE MANIFEST `config`, NOT THE TYPESCRIPT CLASS API. Speed, spawn, look-sensitivity, initial look direction, FOV, slope, jump feel — almost everything a designer reaches for is a config VALUE, not a method. If you inspect the Character/LocomotionAbility class and conclude "no setting for X exists", you looked in the wrong place — re-read the manifest `config`. Set values two ways: initial via `Character.create({ config: { locomotion: { runSpeed: 7 }, character: { spawn:{x,z,facingDeg}, camera:{ mode, lookSensitivity } } } })`, or live via `character.config.set("ns.key", value)` (read every tick — use it for timed buffs, difficulty). In humanoid-character 0.2.21+, omit/null camera.initialYaw to derive the behind-character camera from spawn.facingDeg; numeric initialYaw explicitly overrides that camera seed. Runtime-only actions (teleport/applyImpulse/respawn/setEnabled/camera.setYaw/addTrauma) are in `capabilities.api`. The character-world recipe has worked examples (timed speed-boost, camera re-face, top-down/2.5D).
MATCH THE CONTROLS TO THE GENRE — every `allow*` gate DEFAULTS TO ON, so you must DISABLE what does not fit, or the player keeps a control the game should not have. A first-person game MUST set `character.camera.allowModeToggle:false` or pressing T still flips to third-person; top-down sets `allowRotate:false`+`allowZoom:false`; a no-jump walking sim/puzzle sets `locomotion.allowJump:false`. Pick the camera mode AND lock the gates that contradict it whenever you configure a character.
A WORLD WHERE PLAYERS SHOOT IS A SOLVED RECIPE — never hand-build gunplay from primitives. The platform ships the whole stack: the gun-control ability (stance/ADS/fire modes/ammo/recoil), weapon profiles (a gun is DATA — a mesh + a category is playable), FX/hit systems with a spread crosshair, server-validated damage (the one-claim rule; gun-declared damage via weaponItems + the weaponDamage op — a client never names a number), health/death/respawn driven by room rules, and a death ragdoll that is also a world mechanic (character.ragdoll.enter/exit). Read read_doc({name:"shooter-worlds"}) for the client half and read_template({name:"shooter-range"}) for the room half BEFORE designing any combat world.
NPCS ARE CHARACTERS, NOT PROPS: a shopkeeper, a quest giver, a guard or a monster that hunts the player is built on the SAME humanoid-character chassis the player uses — an NPC is a Character whose driver is your world logic instead of the keyboard. NpcScene builds and owns each one (model clone, private input router, body, nameplate, teardown), an AIDriver behaviour steers it (seek/stop/face/jump plus whisker avoidance and a stuck commit), InteractionSpots gives it a walk-up-and-press-interact prompt, and NavGrid routes it around the level geometry your own colliders already describe. Never hand-roll a creature out of meshes and lerps, and never invent an NPC API: read read_doc({name:"npc-world"}) BEFORE building one and confirm every call against get_package_manifest("humanoid-character") capabilities.api. AN NPC CAN ALSO HOLD AND FIRE A REAL GUN — the same gun-control ability, weapon profiles, FX and hit systems the player uses, with cadence, damage, magazine, engage range and line of sight all owned by your behaviour loop; npc-world.md teaches the arming recipe (replica mode, inside the decorate hook) and the automatic damage flinches every character already carries. VERIFY BY MEASURING, NOT BY LOOKING: hand the pool to the inspect lane (`world.ready({ scene, body, spawn, npcs, npcState })`) and run inspect_npc — distance walked vs gained, stuck windows, arrived edges, the state timelines — then capture_npc ONCE to look; every NPC failure mode here is silent and a still frame shows none of them. Two traps whose symptoms are silent, both spelled out there: an NPC on the default stand body never walks (movement intent is inert by design), and a MOVING npc in a multiplayer world must belong to the room — NpcScene NPCs are client-local, so the room drives it and humanoidEntities renders it (read_template({name:"npc-wave"})). A standing NPC needs no server involvement at all.
WIRE WORLD INPUT THROUGH THE INPUT ROUTER, NOT addEventListener — the character system ships a standard action set (move/look/jump/interact/… + pause/menu actions) with keyboard+gamepad bindings; the full list, the semantic controller map, and the platform-RESERVED keys live in get_package_manifest("humanoid-character") `capabilities` (actions / controller / reservedKeys). Bind the STANDARD ids first (interact/primary/secondary/ability1-9 + the equip cycle/melee/emote + the menu set) — the id carries its keyboard+gamepad+touch bindings, so you never pick a key; mint a namespaced custom action (`input.registerAction`) only for something outside the set — the collision rule is about what is REGISTERED in this world, not the registry: never a reserved key, never a source a registered action uses; bindings of ids this world never registers are FREE REAL ESTATE to reuse (a card game has no gunplay — the primary/secondary triggers and the reload/melee/emote buttons and keys are unclaimed there; no equip slots ⇒ bumpers are the home for world cycling verbs and Digit1-9 for direct select; to reuse an always-on source like crouch faceRight, disable its gate first, e.g. locomotion.allowCrouch:false). Gamepad placement ladder: a genre-freed plain button (the DEFAULT — put verbs where hands expect them; PAIRED verbs share one symmetric group: bumperL/R, dpadUp/dpadDown, faceLeft/faceRight, triggerL/triggerR — never split a pair across groups) → dpadUp (always free but a FALLBACK: a lone odd verb, or paired with dpadDown when the emote slot is freed) → a `withModifier` chord for occasional verbs (PLATFORM-RESERVED, never claim: modifier+rightStick = zoom, modifier+bumperR = the standard voicePTT, modifier+bumperL = future voice) → keyboard-only (omit `pad`) for testing/debug conveniences ONLY, since pad+touch players can never reach it. Do not stack chords or exotic keys while freed standard buttons sit idle. Inject ONE world-owned InputService via Character.create/CharacterMultiplayer.create `{ input }`, push/pop the `menu` context for pause/UI so gameplay input goes inert, and NEVER bind the reserved keys (Escape = platform tablet, KeyN = voice push-to-talk, backtick = debug overlay; KeyB is NOT reserved anymore — it is the `point` standard action). Do not conflate an INPUT action (a router key binding) with a multiplayer DECLARED action (`room.sendAction`, the server DSL) — they compose: read the input action, send the declared action. PLAYER-FACING CONTROL TEXT NEVER HARDCODES KEY NAMES — render it with `input.format("Drive with {move} · {interact} to grab")` re-run each frame: bare {actionId} tokens expand to the CURRENT binding for the active device (keyboard "E"/"WASD", pad Xbox-style "X"/"RT"/"Left stick", chords "D-pad Right + RB"), staying correct across device swaps and rebinds; give CUSTOM actions a `label` at registerAction so fallback text reads as a verb. Recipe: character-world §8c.
MOBILE CONTROLS ARE A PLATFORM DEFAULT: the current character scaffold mounts createMobileControls on the same InputService and ships helix.controls.json, giving touch players movement, drag look, concurrent pinch zoom/camera transition, jump and metadata-generated action buttons. Configure labels/order/visibility/placement/theme through its safe options and register custom actions with touch metadata; do not hand-build or copy a second HUD. Keep core move/look/zoom unless the genre deliberately disables one. supportsMobile:true still requires portrait+landscape touch QA for movement, look, pinch, jump and a custom verb, plus desktop/gamepad regression. An equivalent custom controller is allowed only with provider:"custom" in the shipped controls contract and the same InputService/context/cleanup semantics. Recipe: helix-world-build → Touch controls.
RESERVE THE TOP-CENTER FOR PLATFORM CHROME (EVERY world, every kind): the player shell overlays a bar across the top-center of the screen (~top 56px — Exit / Save Progress / helixOS / fullscreen; user-hideable but shown by default). Put your HUD / on-screen UI in a CORNER (top-left/right) or along the BOTTOM — NEVER top-center, or it renders behind the chrome and is unreadable. Full-width or centered elements start ≥64px down (templates place banners ~20% down). The recipe starters pre-place #hud top-left; keep it out of the top-center strip.
PICK THE FOUNDATION: if the world has a player character — ANY camera framing: first-person, third-person, 3D top-down (twin-stick/ARPG/MOBA), 2.5D / side-on (platformer), an avatar that walks/runs/jumps, or behaviors like fly / swim / shoot — build on the humanoid-character system: call get_started({ kind: "character" }). Top-down & 2.5D are just camera/movement config on this system. If players must SEE EACH OTHER or share a game (a hangout, co-op, an arena, a shared-object game) — OR an EXISTING single-player world must become multiplayer — call get_started({ kind: "multiplayer" }) — the hub: a capability-indexed template index (then list_templates + read_template for a complete worked world), the declarative game-logic DSL (read_doc multiplayer-logic), VOICE CHAT — ON BY DEFAULT in every multiplayer world (the recipe declares voice.proximity + the fail-soft join; remove both ONLY for a deliberately silent world; proximity falloff + channels/walkie-talkies/phone calls tune via the manifest multiplayer.voice block), and the single-player→multiplayer CONVERSION guide (authority audit: every local teleport/respawn/round-reset must become a server rule). You write no server code. For a bare scene with no character, get_started({ kind: "scene" }).
THEN BUILD: SCAFFOLD FIRST — call scaffold_world and run the `helix init` command it returns. That writes the whole project (config, manifest, loading screen AND a runnable src/main.ts) already correct; the recipe get_started returns is EXPLANATION of those files, not source to copy. Hand-writing them from prose is a known way to ship a world that builds, validates, and renders nothing. Then: npm install → install_world_packages on the project dir (any world that pins systems/abilities; resolves the pins in-process against THIS environment) → world_metrics on the project dir BEFORE you place geometry (see the next instruction) → npm run build → `helix dev` to DRIVE the build under the SIMULATED shell whenever the world touches purchases, saves or achievements (they answer locally with production caps and a failure-forcing debug menu — read_doc sdk, section Local development) → bake_world_lighting on the project dir when the world is runtime-lit, bounded and static (mode "baked" — see the lighting instruction below; re-run it after any geometry or light change) → validate_world on dist/ and fix every problem → inspect_world on dist/ to verify PLACEMENT by numbers (floating/sunk/intersecting geometry, collider mismatches — findings are measurements to check against your intent, not orders to change the world) → `helix verify-subpath dist` (REQUIRED, see below) → whoami (not logged in? start_login opens the browser sign-in for the human, then check_login) → publish_world on dist/ for the public play link and automatic ready-world cover.
SIZE GEOMETRY FROM world_metrics BEFORE YOU PLACE IT — not after publishing. world_metrics({ projectDir }) reads the traversal envelope out of the world's OWN installed character system: player capsule, STEP HEIGHT (what auto-steps vs what is a wall), max walkable slope, speeds, the derived jump envelope (air time, max flat-ground gap at run and sprint), and corridor/ceiling clearances. Consult it the first time you place a step, ledge, gap, ramp, doorway or ceiling. A world shipped with a 0.42 m step against a 0.35 m limit looked perfect in every screenshot, passed validation, and published with an objective the player physically could not reach — a screenshot cannot show that a player cannot get somewhere, and numbers can. Values are the system DEFAULTS; if you override them in config, size against your own values (get_package_manifest).
NEVER WRITE A ROOT-ABSOLUTE URL INTO A WORLD, AND ALWAYS RUN THE SUB-PATH GATE. A published world is served from a nested path (…/instant-worlds/<id>/<build>/), never the origin root, so any '/helix_modules', '/models/x.glb' or fetch('/data.json') in world code resolves against the SITE root, 404s, and throws — the world renders nothing but an error bar. Resolve against the document instead: new URL('helix_modules/', document.baseURI).href. Keep base: './' in the vite config. And PROVE it with `helix verify-subpath dist` before publishing: npm run preview, validate_world, inspect_world and capture_world_screenshot ALL serve dist/ from an origin root, so every one of them passes a bundle that is broken in production. verify-subpath is the only local gate that serves from a nested path and fails on the throw, the 404, or a blank render.
LIGHTING IS PLATFORM-OWNED BY DEFAULT, WITH A DELIBERATE OPT-OUT: a HELIX world hands its canvas to the visual runtime (createVisualRuntime from the installed `visual` system) and declares HOW it is lit in the FILE public/helix.visuals.json (mode, time of day, grade) — never a hand-placed sun/ambient pair, never a hand-rolled renderer, tone mapper or post stack, and never an inlined config const (the bake patches the FILE). A world that already has its own visual identity — a custom renderer or post chain, a stylized look — may OPT OUT and keep the classic hand-lit doctrine; that is a legitimate deliberate choice, not a defect. For runtime-lit worlds the mode decision matters: BOUNDED, STATIC-GEOMETRY worlds (interiors, arenas, dioramas — nearly every template-class world) ship mode "baked", and BAKED LIGHTING IS A BUILD STEP, NOT A SETTING — bake_world_lighting runs on the BUILT world (minutes of headless GPU work; it flips the mode, writes the artifact and patches the contract into both public/ and the built root), nothing it wrote ships until you re-validate and re-publish, and you RE-BAKE whenever geometry or lights change (no staleness detector exists). Mode "dynamic" is the exception, kept for unbounded/open worlds, very large maps, or worlds whose geometry moves. The whole story: read_doc({name:"lighting-world"}).
WORLD THUMBNAILS: publish_world automatically captures the ready world when no custom cover is selected. Automatic covers refresh with each Build; custom covers are preserved. Declare a hero shot in world code (screenshots.register + screenshots.ready — read_doc({ name: "screenshots" })); for selecting custom media, capture it with capture_world_screenshot, LOOK at the returned image and judge the framing before attaching, then set_world_thumbnail once satisfied. Filling an EMPTY slot is a normal finishing step; never overwrite existing media unless the human explicitly asks. When a change materially alters world visuals, SUGGEST a retake to the human and stop — do not act on it alone.
SEEING YOUR WORLD: measure first, look last. For PLACEMENT — where things are, whether they float/sink/overlap, whether colliders match visuals — use inspect_world: it returns the scene as numbers, and distances read off a screenshot are measurably unreliable (do not answer placement questions by looking harder). capture_world_screenshot is for how the scene READS — framing, materials, lighting, mood — when a change is visual and you cannot otherwise confirm it; skip it for logic-only changes, each capture costs a build + several seconds. A failed capture or inspection is still diagnostic: boot errors from the page are included in the timeout message. If you DO have a live browser tool, prefer it for interactive debugging. Full workflows: read_doc({ name: "world-inspect" }) and read_doc({ name: "screenshots" }). What to look FOR in a capture — and the whole process of taking a raw world from broken assets to looking good (asset defects first, then materials and textures, then composition, taste last) — is read_doc({ name: "world-look" }).
EXISTING WORLD CHECK: when you start working on a world you did not scaffold this session, FIRST run check_for_updates({ projectDir }) before changing anything — it reports stale system pins, missing capabilities (for example a world published before engine-core exists cannot capture screenshots), and inlines the exact steps for each finding. SUGGEST upgrades to the user and stop — never apply a pin change, install, or migration unasked. In-range staleness is fixed by rerunning install_world_packages once the user agrees; everything else follows read_doc({ name: "upgrades" }). The update check also reports INSPECT WIRING — most existing worlds predate inspect_world and never call world.ready, so placement cannot be measured until that one-line wiring lands (suggest it; it is a tiny additive change). When the task is fixing GEOMETRY or PLACEMENT in an existing world, do not hand-compute positions from source or eyeball stale screenshots — get the wiring in, run inspect_world, and read the numbers.
SOCIAL WORLDS: any world with chairs, couches or beds should register sit/lie spots — one call per seat and the prompt, seated pose, replication and occupancy are all platform defaults (character-world section "Sitting & lying spots" has the coordinate contract: the seat point sits ON the cushion/mattress surface, the occupant faces facingYawDeg, and a lying body puts its head OPPOSITE the facing — face away from the pillow). Emote wheel emotes, paired two-person emotes and voice need no world authoring at all.
